Fulfilment scenarios and configurator options

3 printers, each with a 7-head module

CLASSIC VC ↔ AVC

Classic VC and AVC responsibilities

Both can value characteristics and drive component and operation selection. Classic VC already has constraints and variant tables. AVC adds capabilities such as negative variant tables.

Forecast ownership, PIR consumption, material planning, finite scheduling and delivery remain separate responsibilities. For SBC with configured products, the supported PPAC/CDP checking route also matters. Interface and scenario support must be validated for the target release.

Planning and execution objects

Canon process design decisions

  1. Choose the stock point. Which fixed printer variants, modules or long-lead parts should exist before the order?
  2. Review buffer value. Which shortages and supplier lead-time variations hurt delivery? Which service target justifies extra inventory? Inventory optimization and other capabilities should follow that business need.
  3. Choose the forecast and consumption level. Model, stockable variant, module, plant, customer and time window. Avoid counting the same demand twice.
  4. Agree integration ownership. Are we transferring demand as PIRs, handing over IBP planned orders, or combining explicitly separated scopes? Who owns each material and horizon? How do orders, delivery and execution updates return?
  5. Choose the final-assembly planning scope. Does assembly capacity constrain the service date? Compare module-only PP/DS with modules plus final assembly, then validate the supported promise integration.
  6. Agree confirmation policies. Decide whether allocation, allowed alternatives or backorder reprioritisation are needed; validate their compatibility with the configured-product checking route.
  7. Validate two real printer cases. Trace configuration, BOM/routing selection, critical resources and the customer promise. Validate SBC/PPAC/CDP for the configured printer in the selected release.
